chapters.name: Knowing Our Numbers
chapters.explanation: Numbers help us count and compare things. Every digit in a number has a place value, such as ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. To compare two numbers, first count their digits: the number with more digits is bigger. If they have the same number of digits, compare them digit by digit from the left. We can also write numbers in ascending order (smallest to largest) or descending order (largest to smallest). Estimation means rounding a number to a nearby, easier number.
keyPoints: Each digit has a place: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.
More digits means a bigger number.
Same number of digits? Compare from the left.
Ascending means small to big. Descending means big to small.
Rounding gives a nearby, easy number.

chapters.name: Whole Numbers
chapters.explanation: Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. They are the natural numbers together with zero. Every whole number has a successor (the number just after it) and every whole number except 0 has a predecessor (the number just before it). Whole numbers can be shown on a number line. Addition and multiplication of whole numbers follow useful properties: order does not matter (commutative), grouping does not matter (associative), and multiplication distributes over addition.
keyPoints: Whole numbers start at 0: 0, 1, 2, 3 ...
Successor means the next number. Predecessor means the number before.
0 has no whole-number predecessor.

chapters.name: Playing With Numbers
chapters.explanation: A factor of a number divides it exactly with no remainder. A multiple of a number is what you get when you multiply it by 1, 2, 3 and so on. A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two factors. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. Divisibility rules help us check quickly: a number is divisible by 2 if it is even, by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5, by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3, and by 10 if it ends in 0.

A multiple is the number times 1, 2, 3 ...
A prime number has only two factors: 1 and itself.

chapters.name: Basic Geometrical Ideas
chapters.explanation: Geometry studies shapes and space. A point marks an exact location. A line segment is the straight path between two points and has a fixed length. A line goes on forever in both directions, while a ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. Two lines that meet are called intersecting lines; lines that never meet are parallel. A polygon is a closed shape made of line segments, such as a triangle (3 sides) or a quadrilateral (4 sides). A circle is a shape where every point is the same distance from the centre.
keyPoints: A point shows an exact place.
A line segment has two end points.
A ray has one end point and goes on forever.
Parallel lines never meet.

chapters.name: Fractions
chapters.explanation: A fraction shows a part of a whole. In the fraction 3/4, the top number (numerator) tells how many parts we have, and the bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into. Equivalent fractions show the same amount, like 1/2 and 2/4. A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than the denominator. To compare fractions with the same denominator, compare the numerators.

Numerator: parts we have. Denominator: total equal parts.

chapters.name: Components of Food
chapters.explanation: Food contains nutrients that our body needs. The main nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. Carbohydrates and fats give us energy. Proteins help the body grow and repair itself. Vitamins and minerals protect us from diseases. Food also contains dietary fibre (roughage), which helps digestion, and water. A balanced diet has all these nutrients in the right amounts. Not getting enough of a nutrient for a long time can cause deficiency diseases.

chapters.name: Separation of Substances
chapters.explanation: We often need to separate mixtures to remove unwanted parts or collect useful ones. Handpicking removes large impurities like stones from grain. Threshing separates grain from stalks, and winnowing uses wind to separate light husk from heavier grain. Sieving separates particles of different sizes. Sedimentation lets heavy particles settle, decantation pours off the clear liquid, and filtration passes a liquid through a filter to remove solids. Evaporation turns water into vapour and leaves the dissolved solid, such as salt, behind.

Winnowing uses wind to remove husk.

chapters.name: Motion and Measurement of Distances
chapters.explanation: Measurement means comparing a quantity with a standard unit. The standard unit of length is the metre (m). 1 metre = 100 centimetres, 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres, and 1 kilometre = 1000 metres. Using body parts like hand spans gives different results for different people, which is why standard units are needed. Motion means change in position over time. In rectilinear motion an object moves in a straight line, in circular motion it moves along a circle, and in periodic motion it repeats its movement after a fixed time.

chapters.name: Fun with Magnets
chapters.explanation: A magnet attracts materials like iron, nickel and cobalt; these are called magnetic materials. Materials like wood, plastic and paper are non-magnetic. Every magnet has two poles, a north pole and a south pole, and its attraction is strongest at the poles. Like poles repel each other and unlike poles attract. A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest in the north–south direction, which is how a compass works. Magnets lose their magnetism if they are heated, hammered or dropped.

chapters.name: Electricity and Circuits
chapters.explanation: Electricity is a form of energy that lights bulbs and runs fans. An electric cell has a positive and a negative terminal. A bulb glows only when there is a complete path, called a closed circuit, from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, and back to the other terminal. A switch opens or closes the circuit. Materials that let electricity pass through, like copper and iron, are conductors; materials that do not, like plastic, rubber and wood, are insulators.

A bulb glows only in a closed circuit.
A switch opens or closes the circuit.

Transparent objects such as clear glass let light pass through, translucent objects such as butter paper let some light pass, and opaque objects such as wood block light completely. A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light. A mirror reflects light, which changes its direction; that is how we see our image in a mirror.

chapters.name: Nouns
chapters.explanation: A noun is a naming word. It names a person, place, animal, thing or idea. Proper nouns name a particular person, place or thing and always begin with a capital letter, like Riya or Delhi. Common nouns name any person, place or thing, like girl or city. Collective nouns name a group, like a flock of birds. Abstract nouns name ideas or feelings that we cannot touch, like happiness or honesty. Most nouns form their plural by adding -s or -es.

A reflexive pronoun such as myself or themselves refers back to the subject.

chapters.name: Verbs and Tenses
chapters.explanation: A verb is an action or doing word, like run, eat or write. Some verbs show a state, like is, am, are. Tense tells us when an action happens. Present tense shows an action happening now or regularly (she walks). Past tense shows an action that already happened (she walked). Future tense shows an action that will happen (she will walk). Many verbs form the past tense by adding -ed, but irregular verbs change in other ways, like go → went and eat → ate.

chapters.name: The Earth in the Solar System
chapters.explanation: The solar system is made up of the Sun and everything that moves around it: eight planets, their moons, asteroids and comets. The Sun is a star that gives heat and light. The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Earth is the third planet and the only one known to support life, because it has air, water and the right temperature. The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and takes about 27 days to go around the Earth.

chapters.name: Globe: Latitudes and Longitudes
chapters.explanation: A globe is a small model of the Earth. Imaginary lines drawn on the globe help us find places. Lines running east to west are called latitudes, or parallels. The most important latitude is the Equator at 0°, which divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Lines running from the North Pole to the South Pole are called longitudes, or meridians. The Prime Meridian at 0° passes through Greenwich in England. Together, latitudes and longitudes form a grid to locate any place.

chapters.name: Early Humans: From Hunting to Farming
chapters.explanation: Long ago, early humans lived as hunter-gatherers. They hunted animals, caught fish and gathered fruits, roots and nuts. They moved from place to place in search of food and water. They made tools from stone, wood and bone, and discovered how to use fire for warmth, light and cooking. Slowly, people began to grow crops and tame animals. Farming allowed them to stay in one place, so they built homes and formed the first villages.

chapters.name: Motions of the Earth
chapters.explanation: The Earth has two main motions. Rotation is the spinning of the Earth on its axis; one rotation takes about 24 hours and causes day and night. The half facing the Sun has day, while the other half has night. Revolution is the movement of the Earth around the Sun; one revolution takes about 365¼ days, which makes a year. Because the Earth's axis is tilted, different parts receive different amounts of sunlight during the year, which causes the seasons.

chapters.explanation: Perimeter is the total distance around a closed shape. Area is the amount of surface a shape covers, measured in square units. chapters.explanation: Green plants make their own food, so they are called autotrophs. They do this through photosynthesis, which happens mainly in the leaves. chapters.explanation: Respiration is the process by which living things break down food to release energy. chapters.name: Electric Current and its Effects

A fuse is a safety device with a wire that melts and breaks the circuit if too much current flows. When current flows through a wire, the wire behaves like a magnet; this magnetic effect is used in electromagnets and electric bells. chapters.name: Rational Numbers
chapters.explanation: A rational number is any number that can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. All integers and fractions are rational numbers. Rational numbers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, which means the result is always rational. Zero is the additive identity (adding 0 changes nothing) and 1 is the multiplicative identity. The additive inverse of a/b is −a/b, and the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of a/b is b/a. Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many rational numbers.

Food can be preserved from microbes by heating, refrigeration, salting and using preservatives.

Non-metals such as sulphur, carbon and oxygen are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors. Metals react with oxygen to form basic oxides, while non-metals form acidic oxides. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

chapters.name: Sound
chapters.explanation: Sound is produced by vibrating objects. It needs a medium — a solid, liquid or gas — to travel, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. In humans, sound is produced by the vibration of the vocal cords in the voice box (larynx), and we hear when sound makes the eardrum vibrate. The number of vibrations per second is the frequency, measured in hertz (Hz). A higher frequency gives a higher pitch, and a bigger amplitude gives a louder sound. Humans can hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Unwanted loud sound is noise, which causes noise pollution.

chapters.name: Subject–Verb Agreement
chapters.explanation: The verb in a sentence must agree with its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb (She plays), and a plural subject takes a plural verb (They play). Human-made resources, such as buildings and machines, are made by people using natural resources. Human resource means people with knowledge and skills. chapters.name: Matter in Our Surroundings
chapters.explanation: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It is made of tiny particles that have spaces between them, are always moving, and attract each other. Changing temperature or pressure changes the state of matter. The temperature at which a solid melts is its melting point, and at which a liquid boils is its boiling point. Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature and causes cooling.

chapters.explanation: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. A molecule is two or more atoms joined together, such as O₂ or H₂O. Elements are represented by symbols, like H for hydrogen and Na for sodium. The law of conservation of mass states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. One mole of any substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number).

chapters.explanation: Atoms are made of three sub-atomic particles. Protons are positively charged and neutrons have no charge; both are in the small, dense nucleus at the centre. The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n², so K holds 2 and L holds 8. The electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different mass numbers.

chapters.name: Is Matter Around Us Pure?
chapters.explanation: A pure substance has only one kind of particle, such as an element (like gold) or a compound (like water). A mixture contains two or more substances not chemically combined, such as air or salt water. Homogeneous mixtures (solutions) have a uniform composition; heterogeneous mixtures do not. A solution has a solute dissolved in a solvent. A suspension has particles that settle, and a colloid has particles that stay spread out and scatter light (the Tyndall effect). Mixtures can be separated by methods like evaporation, filtration, distillation and chromatography.

Prokaryotic cells, like bacteria, have no true nucleus, while eukaryotic cells have a nucleus bound by a membrane. Organelles do special jobs: mitochondria release energy and are called the powerhouse of the cell, ribosomes make proteins, and plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts.

Infectious diseases are caused by microbes such as viruses, bacteria, fungi and protozoa and can spread from person to person through air, water, food, touch or carriers like mosquitoes. chapters.explanation: Sentences can be grouped by purpose. A declarative sentence makes a statement and ends with a full stop. An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark. Sentences can also be grouped by structure: a simple sentence has one independent clause, a compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a conjunction such as 'and' or 'but', and a complex sentence has an independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

chapters.name: Heredity
chapters.explanation: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring. Gregor Mendel studied pea plants and found that traits are controlled by factors, now called genes, which come in pairs. One form of a gene can be dominant and hide the other, recessive, form. In a cross between pure tall (TT) and pure short (tt) plants, all first-generation plants are tall (Tt). When these are self-crossed, the second generation shows a 3 : 1 ratio of tall to short plants. In humans, sex is determined by chromosomes: females have XX and males have XY, so the father's sperm decides the sex of the child.

chapters.name: Our Environment
chapters.explanation: An ecosystem includes living (biotic) components like plants, animals and microbes and non-living (abiotic) components like air, water and soil. Producers, mainly green plants, make food using sunlight. Consumers eat other organisms, and decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. A food chain shows who eats whom, and connected food chains form a food web. Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next (the 10% law). Harmful chemicals can build up along a food chain, which is called biological magnification. Ozone in the upper atmosphere protects us from UV rays and is damaged by CFCs.

Asexual reproduction involves one parent and produces offspring identical to the parent; methods include binary fission (Amoeba), budding (Hydra, yeast), fragmentation (Spirogyra), spore formation (bread mould) and vegetative propagation (potato, rose cuttings). The secondary sector turns raw materials into products through manufacturing. The tertiary (service) sector provides services such as transport, banking, education and health. GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced in a year. In India, the tertiary sector produces the largest share of GDP, but the primary sector still employs the most people, which shows underemployment. Jobs can also be organised (regular, with benefits) or unorganised (irregular, low protection).

chapters.name: Sets
chapters.explanation: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called elements. Sets can be written in roster form, like {1, 2, 3}, or set-builder form, like {x : x is a natural number less than 4}. The empty set ∅ has no elements. A is a subset of B if every element of A is in B. The union A ∪ B contains elements in A or B, the intersection A ∩ B contains elements in both, and the difference A − B contains elements in A but not in B. A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, and n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

The basic identity is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. The signs of the functions depend on the quadrant: all are positive in the first quadrant, only sine in the second, only tangent in the third, and only cosine in the fourth (All–Sin–Tan–Cos). Sine and cosine have period 2π. Compound angle formulas include sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.

chapters.name: Permutations and Combinations
chapters.explanation: The fundamental principle of counting says that if one event can happen in m ways and another in n ways, both can happen in m × n ways. n! A combination is a selection where order does not matter: ⁿCᵣ = n! / [r!(n − r)!]. Choosing a team is a combination, while arranging people in a line is a permutation. Note that ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.

chapters.name: Sequences and Series
chapters.explanation: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers, and a series is the sum of its terms. In a geometric progression (GP), each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a fixed number called the common ratio r. The nth term is aₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1. If |r| < 1, the infinite GP has a finite sum S = a/(1 − r). The arithmetic mean of a and b is (a + b)/2 and the geometric mean is √(ab); AM ≥ GM for positive numbers.

The distance between two points is √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]. A horizontal line has slope 0 and a vertical line has an undefined slope.

chapters.name: Units and Measurements
chapters.explanation: A physical quantity is expressed as a number times a unit. The International System of Units (SI) has seven base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance) and candela (luminous intensity). Other units are derived from these, like the newton (kg m s⁻²). Dimensional analysis expresses quantities in terms of base dimensions such as [M], [L] and [T]; it helps check equations and convert units. Significant figures show the precision of a measurement, and every measurement has some error.

chapters.name: Motion in a Straight Line
chapters.explanation: Motion along a straight line is described by position, displacement, velocity and acceleration. Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time, while instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular moment, given by v = dx/dt. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt. For uniformly accelerated motion: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², and v² = u² + 2as. On a position–time graph the slope is velocity, and on a velocity–time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the curve is displacement. Freely falling bodies have acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward.

chapters.name: Laws of Motion
chapters.explanation: Newton's first law defines inertia: a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. The second law states that the net force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt = ma for constant mass. Impulse is force × time and equals the change in momentum. Newton's third law says forces always occur in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies. The law of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of an isolated system stays constant. Friction opposes relative motion; static friction is usually greater than kinetic friction. For circular motion, a centripetal force mv²/r is needed.

chapters.name: Work, Energy and Power
chapters.explanation: Work done by a constant force is W = F·s·cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement; no work is done if they are perpendicular. The work–energy theorem says the net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy. Kinetic energy is ½mv², and gravitational potential energy is mgh; the elastic potential energy of a spring is ½kx². When only conservative forces act, mechanical energy is conserved. Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t = F·v. In an elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision, only momentum is conserved.

chapters.name: Structure of Atom
chapters.explanation: Thomson proposed the plum pudding model, and Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed that an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Bohr's model said electrons move in fixed energy levels and emit or absorb energy when they jump between them. The modern quantum mechanical model describes electrons by orbitals and four quantum numbers: principal (n), azimuthal (l), magnetic (m) and spin (s). Electrons fill orbitals by the Aufbau principle (lowest energy first), Pauli's exclusion principle (at most two electrons with opposite spins per orbital) and Hund's rule (orbitals of the same energy are filled singly first).

chapters.name: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
chapters.explanation: Atoms bond to achieve a stable electron arrangement, often an octet. Ionic bonds form when electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal, creating oppositely charged ions, as in NaCl. Covalent bonds form when atoms share electron pairs, as in H₂ and Cl₂. Lewis structures show valence electrons as dots. VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape from electron-pair repulsion: CO₂ is linear, BF₃ is trigonal planar, CH₄ is tetrahedral and H₂O is bent. Hybridisation mixes atomic orbitals, for example sp³ in methane. Hydrogen bonding explains water's high boiling point.

chapters.name: Thermodynamics
chapters.explanation: Thermodynamics studies energy changes. A system is the part being studied and the surroundings are everything else. The first law states that energy is conserved: ΔU = q + w. chapters.name: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
chapters.explanation: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in which a cell grows and divides. It has interphase, where the cell grows and copies its DNA (G₁, S and G₂ phases), and the M phase, where division occurs. Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells and has four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis. Mitosis helps growth and repair. chapters.name: Relations and Functions
chapters.explanation: A relation from set A to set B is a subset of A × B. A relation on a set is reflexive if every element is related to itself, symmetric if aRb implies bRa, and transitive if aRb and bRc imply aRc. A relation with all three properties is an equivalence relation. A function assigns exactly one output to each input. A function is one-one (injective) if different inputs give different outputs, and onto (surjective) if every element of the codomain is an output. A function that is both one-one and onto is bijective and has an inverse. The composition (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)).

chapters.explanation: Biotechnology uses living organisms or their parts to make useful products. Genetic engineering changes an organism's DNA. Restriction enzymes act as molecular scissors, cutting DNA at specific sequences and often leaving sticky ends. DNA ligase joins DNA fragments. A vector, such as a plasmid, carries the desired gene into a host cell like E. coli, creating recombinant DNA. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) makes millions of copies of a DNA segment through cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size. Bioreactors grow large quantities of cells to produce products like insulin.

chapters.name: Evolution
chapters.explanation: Evolution is the gradual change in living organisms over many generations. Evidence comes from fossils, comparative anatomy (homologous organs like the forelimbs of humans, whales and bats, which have the same structure but different functions), and molecular similarities in DNA and proteins. Analogous organs, such as the wings of birds and insects, do the same job but have different structures. Darwin's theory of natural selection states that individuals with variations that help them survive and reproduce pass on those traits. Industrial melanism in peppered moths is a classic example of natural selection.

chapters.name: Human Health and Disease
chapters.explanation: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Diseases caused by pathogens are infectious: typhoid (bacterium Salmonella typhi), malaria (protozoan Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes), common cold (rhinoviruses) and ringworm (fungi). Immunity is the body's ability to fight infection; innate immunity is present from birth, while acquired immunity develops after exposure or vaccination. Antibodies are proteins made by B-lymphocytes that fight antigens. AIDS is caused by HIV, which attacks helper T-cells. Drug and alcohol abuse seriously damage health.

chapters.name: Vocabulary in Context
chapters.explanation: Understanding a word from its context means using the surrounding words and sentences to work out its meaning. Clues can be a definition, a synonym (a word with a similar meaning), an antonym (a word with the opposite meaning), an example or the general sense of the passage. Knowing prefixes and suffixes also helps: 'un-', 'dis-' and 'in-' often mean 'not', while '-ful' means 'full of' and '-less' means 'without'. A good vocabulary makes reading easier and writing more precise.

Confusing homophones is common: 'their' (belonging to them), 'there' (a place) and 'they're' (they are); 'its' (belonging to it) and 'it's' (it is). chapters.name: Database Concepts and SQL

DDL commands like CREATE TABLE define structure; DML commands like INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data; and SELECT retrieves data. WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts them, and aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM and AVG summarise data, often with GROUP BY.

chapters.name: Introduction to Macroeconomics
chapters.explanation: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, including total output, employment, inflation and the general price level. It became important after the Great Depression of 1929, when unemployment rose sharply; John Maynard Keynes's ideas shaped modern macroeconomics. An economy has four sectors: households, firms, government and the external sector (rest of the world). In the circular flow of income, households supply factors of production to firms and receive factor income (rent, wages, interest and profit), and spend it on goods and services produced by firms. Goods can be final goods, used for consumption or investment, or intermediate goods, used up in producing other goods.

chapters.name: National Income Accounting

chapters.name: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rate

The current account includes trade in goods (exports and imports), services, and transfers such as remittances. The capital account includes foreign investment, loans and borrowings. A trade deficit occurs when imports exceed exports. The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as ₹83 per US dollar. When the rupee depreciates, imports become costlier and exports become cheaper for foreigners. Exchange rates can be fixed, flexible (set by the market) or managed.
